# Chapter 12: Performance Tuning and Optimization

Achieving maximum performance from modern server silicon requires aligning the operating system's software settings with the underlying CPU microarchitecture, memory channels, and I/O bus topology.

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS introduces transformative hardware optimizations: optimized **`amd64-v3` architecture builds**, high-frequency **low-latency kernel packages**, the **BBRv3** TCP congestion control algorithm, and kernel **Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO)** via Sysprof.

This chapter details the performance tuning parameters, sysctl controls, and profiling techniques required to extract optimal throughput and minimal tail latency from production systems.

---

## Understanding System Performance Bottlenecks

Performance bottlenecks manifest across four foundational system resources:

| Subsystem | Primary Metrics to Monitor | Saturation Indicators | Primary Bottleneck Causes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **CPU** | `%usr`, `%sys`, Run Queue Length | High load average, context switching | Inefficient algorithms, lock contention |
| **Memory** | PSI (`/proc/pressure/memory`), Page Faults | `allocstall`, high anonymous paging | Working set exceeds physical RAM, leaks |
| **Storage I/O** | `r/s`, `w/s`, `%util`, `await` (ms) | High queue depth, I/O wait CPU | Unaligned I/O, synchronous fsync thrashing |
| **Network** | Packet drops, TCP retransmits | High socket buffer backlog | Saturated link, small TCP windows, bufferbloat |

---

## CPU Scheduling and Low-Latency Kernels

For workloads demanding microsecond determinism—such as audio workstations, high-frequency trading engines, and edge robotics—standard generic kernels favor throughput at the expense of scheduling latency.

Ubuntu provides specialized low-latency kernels:

```bash
# Install the official low-latency kernel
sudo apt install -y linux-lowlatency

# Inspect scheduling preemption model
uname -v | grep PREEMPT
```

### CPU Frequency Governor Tuning
Ensure cores do not dynamically throttle during latency-critical processing:
```bash
# Set CPU scaling governor to 'performance' across all cores
sudo apt install -y cpufrequtils
sudo cpupower frequency-set -g performance

# Verify clock speeds
cpupower frequency-info
```

## Memory Management and Swap Tuning

Tune kernel virtual memory behavior via `/etc/sysctl.d/99-performance-memory.conf`:

```ini
# /etc/sysctl.d/99-performance-memory.conf

# Bias against swapping anonymous memory (default is 60; set to 10 for servers)
vm.swappiness = 10

# Percentage of RAM allocated to dirty page caching before background writeback begins
vm.dirty_background_ratio = 5

# Maximum percentage of RAM that can be dirty before allocating threads stall
vm.dirty_ratio = 10

# Increase maximum memory map regions for high-thread databases
vm.max_map_count = 1048576

# Transparent Huge Pages: enable madvise to let runtimes manage hugepages explicitly
# (echo madvise | sudo tee /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled)
```
Apply settings:
```bash
sudo sysctl --system
```

---

## Disk I/O Optimization and Storage Schedulers

Modern NVMe SSDs utilize thousands of hardware submission and completion queues, rendering legacy multi-path elevators obsolete:

```bash
# Verify active I/O scheduler for NVMe drive
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler
# [none] mq-deadline kyber bfq
```

- **`none`**: Standard for fast NVMe SSDs. Delivers maximum parallel IOPS directly to hardware queues without kernel scheduling overhead.
- **`mq-deadline`**: Recommended for enterprise SATA SSDs and cloud block volumes.
- **`bfq`**: Recommended for rotating mechanical HDDs to prevent desktop stuttering during background transfers.

Set scheduler persistently via udev rule `/etc/udev/rules.d/60-io-schedulers.rules`:
```text
ACTION=="add|change", KERNEL=="nvme[0-9]*", ATTR{queue/scheduler}="none"
ACTION=="add|change", KERNEL=="sd[a-z]", ATTR{queue/rotational}=="0", ATTR{queue/scheduler}="mq-deadline"
```

## Network Performance Tuning with `sysctl` and BBRv3

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS includes **BBRv3 (Bottleneck Bandwidth and RTT)**—Google's state-of-the-art model-based congestion control algorithm designed to maximize throughput over lossy and high-latency links:

Harden `/etc/sysctl.d/99-performance-network.conf`:

```ini
# Enable BBRv3 congestion control and fair queueing
net.core.default_qdisc = fq
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control = bbr

# Increase maximum socket receive and transmit buffers (64 MB for 40/100GbE)
net.core.rmem_max = 67108864
net.core.wmem_max = 67108864

# Configure TCP autotuning buffer windows (min, default, max bytes)
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096 87380 67108864
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem = 4096 65536 67108864

# Increase listen backlog queue for high-concurrency web services
net.core.somaxconn = 65535
net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 32768

# Enable TCP Fast Open (client + server)
net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen = 3

# Disable slow start restart to prevent window collapse on idle sockets
net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle = 0
```
Apply:
```bash
sudo sysctl --system
```

## `systemd` Performance Optimization

Measure and shave seconds from server startup times:

```bash
# Analyze total boot time breakdown (firmware, loader, kernel, userspace)
systemd-analyze
# Startup finished in 1.412s (firmware) + 0.980s (loader) + 1.204s (kernel) + 2.812s (userspace) = 6.408s

# Identify the slowest services delaying boot
systemd-analyze blame | head -n 10

# Generate an SVG critical-chain timeline waterfall diagram
systemd-analyze plot > boot_timeline.svg
```

Disable unneeded services (e.g., modemmanager or bluetooth on headless cloud instances):
```bash
sudo systemctl disable --now ModemManager.service bluetooth.service
```

## `amd64-v3` Architecture Variants

Standard Linux packages are built against the generic `x86-64-v1` or `x86-64-v2` baselines to maintain compatibility with 15-year-old CPUs.

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS provides optimized package repositories compiled specifically for the **`x86-64-v3`** microarchitecture level:
- Requires AVX, AVX2, BMI1, BMI2, FMA, and MOVBE instruction sets (present on Intel Haswell / AMD Zen 1 and newer).
- Recompiled libraries (`glibc`, OpenSSL, Python, Go) execute vector instructions directly without runtime CPU dispatch branches.
- Delivers **10% to 25% throughput gains** across cryptographic operations, mathematical processing, and database lookups.

Verify if your hardware supports `x86-64-v3`:
```bash
/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --help | grep -A 5 "Subdirectories of glibc-hwcaps"
```

---

## Profile-Guided Optimization with `Sysprof`

Profile your production binaries under real-world traffic to discover hot code paths:

```bash
# Record system-wide performance profile using Sysprof CLI
sudo sysprof-cli -c -d 15 -o production.syscap

# Inspect symbol CPU consumption
sysprof-cli -d production.syscap
```

---

## Chapter Summary

- Performance engineering requires identifying saturation across CPU, memory, storage, and networking.
- Low-latency kernels and static performance governors eliminate scheduling delays for real-time services.
- `vm.swappiness` and dirty writeback ratios balance page cache I/O against memory exhaustion.
- NVMe drives achieve maximum IOPS when configured with the `none` multi-queue scheduler.
- BBRv3 congestion control and enlarged TCP socket buffers deliver superior network throughput.
- Modern `amd64-v3` repositories deliver 10%–25% performance boosts by harnessing AVX2 vector extensions.
